extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, scholars, media critics, and practicing journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and informal rules used by national news organizations (network evening newscasts and weekly newsmagazines) to decide what to cover and how to report it. Focuses on news values, organizational constraints, source and audience influences, and normative prescriptions (e.g., multiperspectival news).

rubrics_metrics.name: News values / What makes something 'news'
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying topical values and considerations journalists use to judge newsworthiness (e.g., order vs. disorder, leadership, prominence, conflict, novelty, human interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes emphasis on 'Knowns' (especially government) and 'Unknowns' (conflict, lawbreaking, unusual activities). Journalists favor stories that fit shared topical values such as order/leadership and moral/social disorder; these choices shape both selection and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability and suitability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event or statement is suitable to be reported given medium, audience, time/space constraints and journalistic priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitability considerations include action, clarity, completeness, freshness, pace, product constraints, sources, and substantive importance. Suitability determines which among many available stories are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive considerations (importance judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments about how important or significant a story is (e.g., national political/economic happenings, foreign crises with American involvement, scandals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive factors determine leads and cover stories; consider scope, consequences, leadership involvement, and relation to enduring national values when ranking importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source considerations (articulateness, authoritativeness, availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of sources based on articulateness, authoritativeness, availability, geographic/social proximity, reliability, and trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists depend on regular, authoritative official sources; availability and accessibility often trump theoretical accuracy. Source power influences story selection and framing; access to top editors/producers matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience considerations (size, demographics, tastes)
rubrics_metrics.description: How perceptions of the audience (who they are, what they want) affect story selection and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations aim to hold/expand audiences (esp. 18–34 for advertisers) and therefore increase soft/feature stories when needed. Despite this, journalists often assume an audience like themselves and may shun systematic audience research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial / advertiser pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of profits, budgets, conglomeration, and advertisers on editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertiser and profit pressures can reduce budgets, close bureaus, change formats, and cause avoidance of stories that risk ad revenue; top editors negotiate these tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and product considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational and production constraints (deadlines, limited time/space, costs) that structure story selection and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight schedules and constrained 'news holes' (e.g., 22–23 minutes of TV news) force use of temporal pegs, pre-scheduled sections, and editing trade-offs; efficiency often shapes which stories survive editorial filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format / medium considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: How the medium (TV evening news vs. weekly newsmagazine) shapes the kinds of stories chosen and how they are told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV favors filmed, action-packed stories and short 'tell stories' (15–30 seconds) or 1–2 minute filmed segments; magazines favor long narratives, vivid quotes, and illustrated features. Format changes (sections, recurring segments) create pre-scheduled story slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity, values, and ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional commitment to objectivity, fairness, and detachment, and the limits of that commitment given unconscious ideology and professional values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists formally swear by objectivity but may unconsciously incorporate ideological assumptions (e.g., favoring responsible capitalism or mainstream centrist views). Objectivity is practiced as a set of techniques but does not eliminate value implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and inclusion/exclusion (multiperspectival news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations of balance in coverage, whether multiple perspectives are represented, and decisions about inclusion or exclusion of viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is a recurrent editorial criterion; the author argues for 'multiperspectival news' as a policy aim. Inclusion/exclusion involve editorial choices about whose voices are heard and which values are represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste considerations and taboos
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic taste judgments about what is acceptable (e.g., profanity taboo, repetition taboo, sexual/sensational content) and how taste shapes coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top editors apply taste filters to avoid offending audiences or advertisers; taste can operate as self-censorship, and norms shift slowly over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical standards and story quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional norms for clarity, completeness, technical correctness, and overall quality of storytelling and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories are evaluated for technical standards (clarity, pacing, factual accuracy), and must pass hierarchical editorial review (rewrites ordered by top editors). Quality considerations affect length, depth, and use of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection process and organizational influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal and informal processes (meetings, chain of command) through which stories are proposed, selected, edited, and approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top editors/producers, executives, anchors, and news managers play decisive roles; organizational roles and hierarchies shape which pitches move forward. Peer pressures and conformity also affect selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source power and top-down news
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural dependence of journalists on powerful official sources (government, Pentagon, White House) and the 'top-down' character of much national news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When officials can 'stay on message' they shape the news; institutional sources supply steady flows of statements, often simplifying journalists' tasks. This supply dependence explains routine coverage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Pegs / Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporal factors (timeliness, pegs, freshness) determining news selection and prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal pegs and deadlines are essential: events tied to a current time/date get priority. Freshness is often more important than deeper context when space/time are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity / Scoops and investigative thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Value placed on getting exclusive information ('scoops') and limits on investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoops and exclusives are prized; investigative exposes require underlying corruption or wrongdoing to exist and are resource-intensive, so they are constrained by budgets and source availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staged events and pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that many newsworthy events are staged for media (press conferences, orchestrated spectacles) and are treated as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists cover anticipated/staged events; media events can crowd out unscripted reporting and may be restaged for better visuals or narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints on reporting imposed by external pressures (government, advertisers) and internal editorial restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-censorship arises from fears of losing access, advertising, or legal trouble; national security and publisher/owner pressure produce both conscious and unconscious censorship decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story mixture and program/magazine structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial design of each issue or broadcast (mix of hard news, features, back-of-book, segments) that determines which stories fit where.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News programs and magazines arrange leads, cover stories, features and recurring sections to create distinctive identity and predictable slots for certain story types (e.g., 'Person of the Week', 'Your Time').

rubrics_metrics.name: Story length and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about how long to devote to each story and the pacing of transitions (especially relevant to TV's 22–23 minute format).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV items are commonly 1–2 minutes for filmed stories and 15–30 seconds for tell stories; length choices are driven by perceived importance, available airtime, and audience attention patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats, generalists, and reporter roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of reporters to beats vs. use of generalists and how those roles affect coverage and source relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat reporters develop access but may self-censor to protect relationships; generalists pursue varied stories but may rely more on accessible official sources. Recruitment, seniority and morale influence staffing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of audience research (or its neglect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how audience studies inform editorial choices, and the tendency of journalists to ignore systematic research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journalists shun detailed audience research and default to imagining an audience similar to themselves; when audience research is used it can steer content toward demographics prized by advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusionary/exclusionary value judgments (value inclusion/exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial choices that consciously or unconsciously include certain values/voices and exclude others, producing ideological effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value exclusion often operates via editing/highlighting; inclusion of dissenting views is uneven. The book documents ideological editing and house tendencies (radical/conservative) within outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: National values and social representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of national news to reflect mainstream middle-class values and underrepresent working class, poor, and some minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage often privileges elite perspectives and 'leadership' narratives; calls for multiperspectival news argue for broader representation of social classes and ideologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and repetition taboo
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for novel or fresh events and avoidance of repeating the same stories unless new developments occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors avoid 'stale' stories and apply a repetition taboo; only when new angles or exclusive material appears will similar topics be rerun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format change and technological influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of technology (cable, internet, camera miniaturization, digital editing) on news gathering, mobility, and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology increases speed and mobility, enabling live coverage and smaller crews, but has not fundamentally changed core editorial decision rules; web scoops and 24-hour cable alter competition and format choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and political pressures shaping content
rubrics_metrics.description: How political climates, advertiser sensitivities, and social norms influence what topics are pursued or avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic political pressures (e.g., from administrations) and long-term ideological shifts shape which sources are prominent and which policy viewpoints appear in news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service stories and soft news utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'service' and soft/feature news (health, lifestyle) to attract or retain audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft news increases when audiences fragment or shrink; magazines and programs may add lifestyle sections or service journalism to hold segments of the audience attractive to advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality vs. competitive considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing story quality/depth with competition-driven needs for distinctive formats and ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition leads to format innovations and sometimes compromises on depth; executives balance the desire for high-quality journalism with needs for ratings and distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical obligation toward democracy (news policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative criterion that news should strengthen democracy by providing multiperspectival, representative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author advocates news policy oriented to multiperspectival reporting that better represents diverse viewpoints and social groups rather than only mainstream leadership perspectives.
